NOTATION. This follows Dedekind's module calculus as in the next page and in his 1897 and 1900 papers on Dualgruppen.
- a + b is the sum of modules, the 'greatest common divisor'.
- a - b is the intersection a ∩ b, the 'least common multiple'.
- a < b means a is a divisor (Theiler) of b, i.e. a ⊇ b.
- [δ] is the module generated by δ, presumably 𝔬δ for the ring 𝔬 of the next page.
This reading is confirmed internally. The next page writes t_r > a_r, where t_r is a sum of modules b_s that are each contained in a_r, so t_r ⊆ a_r. The modular law in line 1 also only holds in this reading.

BLOCK 1: the modular law and its application.
(1) Line 1 states Dedekind's modular law. If y ⊇ q, then q + (x ∩ y) = (q + x) ∩ y.
(2) Substitute y = a_r, q = m, x = [δ]. The hypothesis a_r ⊇ m holds because m is the l.c.m. of the a_r (next page). This gives m + ([δ] ∩ a_r) = (m + [δ]) ∩ a_r.
(3) 'hier = a_r' asserts that this equals a_r. That requires a_r ⊆ m + [δ], a context assumption not proved on the page.
(4) Write [δ] ∩ a_r = m_r[δ], where m_r = ([δ], a_r) is the quotient ideal {x : xδ ∈ a_r}.
(5) Then d := Σ a_r = Σ (m + m_r[δ]) = m + [δ](m_1 + m_2 + ...).
(6) Dedekind then writes this as m + 𝔪[δ] with 𝔪 = Σ m_r, and finally as m + [δ]. The last step needs 𝔪[δ] = [δ], e.g. 1 ∈ Σ m_r, equivalently δ ∈ d. This is tacit [my filling].
(7) Put n := [δ], so d = m + n.

BLOCK 2: an interval isomorphism (Dedekind's transposition principle).
(8) If b ⊇ m, the modular law gives m + (n ∩ b) = (m + n) ∩ b = d ∩ b.
(9) Hence, if m + n ⊇ b ⊇ m (d < b < m):
  - b = m + (b ∩ n);
  - n ⊇ b ∩ n ⊇ m ∩ n.
(10) Conversely, if n ⊇ b' ⊇ m ∩ n:
  - b' = n ∩ (b' + m), by the modular law with b' ⊆ n: n ∩ (b' + m) = b' + (n ∩ m) = b';
  - m + n ⊇ b' + m ⊇ m.
(11) Restated with t = b ∩ n:
  - From m + n ⊇ b ⊇ m and t = b ∩ n it follows that b = m + t and n ⊇ t ⊇ m ∩ n.
  - From n ⊇ t ⊇ m ∩ n and b = t + m it follows that t = n ∩ b and m + n ⊇ b ⊇ m.
(12) Conclusion: the two 'Doppelannahmen' {m+n ⊇ b ⊇ m, t = b ∩ n} and {n ⊇ t ⊇ m ∩ n, b = t + m} are equivalent. So b ↦ b ∩ n and t ↦ t + m are mutually inverse bijections between the intervals [m, m+n] and [m∩n, n]. Both maps are order preserving, so the intervals are lattice-isomorphic.

PURPOSE. This serves the study of a 'productive' system of modules a_1, ..., a_n and an element δ = Σ β_r (next page). It decomposes the g.c.d. d = Σ a_r as m + [δ]. It then transfers the interval between m and d to the interval between m ∩ [δ] and [δ], presumably to count or describe the intermediate modules via the principal module [δ].
errors: Step 'hier = a_r' tacitly assumes a_r ⊆ m + [δ]; this is not justified on this page.
The passage m + [δ](m_1 + m_2 + ...) = m + 𝔪[δ] = m + [δ] needs 𝔪[δ] = [δ] (e.g. 1 ∈ Σ m_r, or δ ∈ Σ a_r). This is left implicit.

Notational slip: the lines 'b = m + (b - n)' and 'n < b - n < m - n' use b - n (b ∩ n) for what is later called t. These lines are correct, merely notationally loose. The genuine slip is the inline formula 'b = m + (b-n)': it is correct only because of the modular law with d ∩ b = b.
Minor: the converse is written as 'b' = n - (b' + m)', i.e. n ∩ (b' + m). This is correct; there is only a stray parenthesis in the hypothesis line.
Otherwise all lattice-theoretic steps are correct, given the modular law.

results.what: Modular law: if y ⊇ q then q + (x ∩ y) = (q + x) ∩ y, for modules
results.usually_credited_to: Dedekind (1894 Supplement XI / 1897 'Über Zerlegungen von Zahlen durch ihre größten gemeinsamen Teiler')

results.what: Mutually inverse maps b ↦ b ∩ n and t ↦ t + m between the intervals [m, m+n] and [m∩n, n]
results.modern_name: Transposition principle / diamond isomorphism theorem for modular lattices (lattice form of the second isomorphism theorem)

results.what: Decomposition of the g.c.d. of a productive system as d = m + [δ] with [δ] ∩ a_r = (a_r : δ)[δ]
results.modern_name: Module generated by the l.c.m. plus a principal module; ideal quotient (a : δ)

deep.surprise_reason: This is Dedekind's own modular law and the interval-isomorphism (transposition) principle, both published by him in 1897/1900. The page is a working draft of known material, applied to a specific module configuration.

checkable.sympy: all(gcd(q, lcm(x, y)) == lcm(gcd(q, x), y) for q in range(1,40) for x in range(1,40) for y in divisors(q))
checkable.asserts: Modular law in the module lattice of Z (sum = gcd, intersection = lcm, y ⊇ q means y | q)

checkable.sympy: m,n=12,18; [ (b, lcm(b,n), gcd(lcm(b,n),m)) for b in divisors(m) if b % gcd(m,n)==0 ]
checkable.asserts: For gcd(m,n) | b | m: t = lcm(b,n) satisfies n | t | lcm(m,n) and gcd(t,m) = b, i.e. b ↦ b∩n is inverted by t ↦ t+m

checkable.sympy: all(lcm(gcd(t,m), n) == t for m in range(1,30) for n in range(1,30) for t in divisors(lcm(m,n)) if t % n == 0)
checkable.asserts: Converse: for n | t | lcm(m,n), t = n ∩ (t + m), i.e. lcm(gcd(t,m), n) = t
